"Perceiving," writes Gibson, "is a registering of certain definite dimensions of invariance in the stimulus flux, together with definite parameters of disturbance. The invariants specify the persistence of the environment and of oneself. The disturbances specify the changes in the environment and of oneself." I will note in passing that the words "and of oneself" are highly significant, inasmuch as they imply that exteroception and proprioception are complementary and thus inseparable functions. What I wish especially to draw attention to, however, is the fact that there exists, according to Gibsonian theory, a direct perception of persistence, which is something entirely different from the persistence of a perception. Given the far-reaching significance of this fact, it will be well to describe a pivotal experiment supportive of this contention.

The experiment, first performed by G.A. Kaplan in 1969, involves a cinematographic display in which a photograph of a textured surface was altered, frame by frame, so as to produce a dissimilar texture on one side of a moving invisible line. The display was intended to simulate the optical information specifying the progressive occlusion of one surface by another. All observers perceived one surface going behind another, or coming from behind another when the process was reversed. "In short, one surface was seen in a legitimate sense behind another at an occluding edge." When the film was stopped, the edge perception ceased, and was replaced by the perception of one continuous yet divided surface. Now, whatever this result may have suggested to other investigators, Gibson recognized therein a disproof of the classical theory: "For we are not allowed to say that a hidden surface is perceived; we can only say that it is remembered....if an occluded surface is perceived, the doctrine is upset." Gibson insists that an occluded surface can be perceived, that there can in fact be perceptions without corresponding sensations [footnote: discoveries in the field of neurophysiology (e.g. "subjective contours") have since verified Gibson's conclusion]. It is this remarkable claim that we need now to reflect upon. The key to the problem, as we shall see, lies in the recognition that what we perceive are not images, but invariants. The following explanations - which richly deserve to be quoted at length - may help to make this clear:

The old approach to perception took the central problem to be how one could see into the distance and never asked how one could see into the past and future. These were not problems for perception. The past was remembered, and the future was imagined. Perception was of the present. But this theory has never worked....the environment seen-at-this-moment does not constitute the environment that is seen. Neither does the environment seen-from-this-point constitute the environment that is seen....It is obvious that a motionless observer can see the world from a single fixed point of observation and can thus notice the perspective of things. It is not so obvious but it is true that an observer that is moving about sees the world at no point of observation and thus, strictly speaking, cannot notice the perspective of things. The implications are radical....The world is not viewed in perspective. The underlying invariant structure has emerged from the changing perspective structure....It sounds very strange to say that one can perceive an object or a whole habitat at no fixed point of observation, for it contradicts the picture theory of perception and the retinal image doctrine on which it is based....But the notion of ambulatory vision is not more difficult, surely, than the notion of successive snapshots of the flowing optic array taken by the eye and shown in the dark projection room of the skull.

One sees from these remarkable observations that, in Gibson's theory, invariants replace the visual image as the founding conception.

It is to be noted that what may be termed an ecological conception of time is implicit in the Gibsonian theory, a fact of which Gibson himself was keenly aware. What constitutes time, ecologically speaking, are events: "Events are perceived, time is not." Elsewhere Gibson points out that "The stream of experience does not consist of an instantaneous present and a linear past receding into the distance...there is no dividing line between the present and the past, between perceiving and remembering." And let us note: only on this basis could there be a direct perception of persistence and events, as Gibson claims. It seems that time, too, needs to be conceived "on the level appropriate to the study of perception." Even as substances must not be reduced to so-called atoms [Smith has argued that atoms exist only physically, not corporeally, which relegates them to an even lesser ontological level than the corporeal], so too the flux of time, it appears, must not be "atomized" in the manner of physics, that is to say, reduced to "instants" the way a line is reduced to points.

That is the end of the section. The entire chapter goes more into all of these issues (like better explaining what exactly invariants are), but hopefully this is sufficient for now to support my point that, if perception itself is understood as requiring "it's own conception of time", then perhaps we can free ourselves from this universalized conception of time as always a linear series of moments, wherein separation from it would confine us to only a single instant.

Rather, the instant itself is imperceptible, and so what we do perceive is not reducible to these instants. Gibson's claim that not all perception is accompanied with sensation may seem radical at first, but after a moment's thought I think it is almost self-evident. All of the participants in that experiment perceived one surface behind another, even though they could not sense any of the texture data of the surface allegedly behind the other surface, where it was said to be behind. his is indeed a perception of something that is not itself sensed. It is not rightly said to be inferred, either, since it is actually grasped or seen instantly (even though instants themselves are not seen, the act of perception itself remains instantaneous).

Anyway, if we can even shake ourselves a modicum away form the Cartesian conception of time we have, perhaps we can better understand how God could perceive all of "time" at once, without, indeed, seeing only a "still frame", or "nothing at all". God isn't embodied, remember, so all of His perception is without sensation. Pure gnosis, in other words.

And that, surely, is not contrary to free will.

Preliminary: I don't think that perception is truly what's at stake in the problem I laid out in the former comment. I'm going to try to be as brief as possible as it concerns perception. I think the philosophy of perception is fascinating, but it is also some of the most controversial and confusing. I don't pretend to have a confident take on perception.

I'll first say, probably without defending it sufficiently, that I believe the type of perception called direct realism that Smith describes is almost certainly implausible. I tend to fall into the idealist camp, though probably something closer to Kantian idealism. At this point, it's undeniable that at least part of what perception consists in is sense data. I'll mention something briefly that I think makes this obvious. But let's also not forget I'm a big fan of phenomenology, so you do not have to tell me that perception is far more than sense data. I'd highly recommend John Russon's book Human Experience for a good contemporary synthesis on perception that is careful to treat to the experiential and subjective parts of it.

I appreciate Gibson's focus on being an embodied observer within an environment. I actually think his theory does something to counter the objection to realism having to do with perspective distortion. Gibson's ambient optical array and the changing angles of light as the observer moves about an environment are able to explain why the environment appears to change as we move through it, and why standing at one side of a table, for instance, the side closest to us appears longer. But I also think he deludes himself in thinking that we can arrive at an account of perception by relying to this extent on sense data.

We have to be able to distinguish between what we are perceiving and what we are sensing. This is not at all an easy thing to do. It struck me that Gibson mentioned the past and the future in that passage, although I wasn't quite clear on how he was using those concepts. From the phenomenological perspective, our perceptions are always constructed at least in part by the past and by our expectations of the future, such that when I look at a room, what strikes me as the 'present' (or the experience of that room which is presenting itself to me) is never the room in itself, but instead a synthesis of past data and also predictions about the future (in some sense, we are constantly in both past and future in order to have the present field of experience). It felt as though Gibson was touching on this idea.

However, I don't think that we can entirely toss out the photographic character of sense data. I am as keen to reject, as Gibson is, the idea that perception is built on photographic frames of sense data. But in asking the question as to whether we can ever separate what we perceive from what we truly sense, I'd put cameras forward as a useful example. A camera could be thought to encapsulate a purely representational (in a physical sense) way of representing sensation. The reason I'm convinced that there is some photographic component to perception has to do with the way that photographs effect us. Photorealistic image can have profound impact on me. I can be aroused by a picture of a naked woman to, more or less, the same extent (albeit not the same particular quality of arousal) as seeing a woman standing in front of me. In those cases, we believe correctly that the reason this is possible is because the woman in the photograph looks nearly identical (perhaps imperceptibly different) from the real woman, which says to me that the 'visual' content of my perception of real women is at least in part captured by photographs.

But to demonstrate that Gibson's theory doesn't quite capture all of the phenomena involved in perception, we could cite any number of optical illusions. Take the old woman-young woman illusion:

https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Kirk_Stamant/publication/233626368/figure/fig1/AS:300058999312388@1448551048203/The-optical-illusion-The-Young-Girl-Old-Woman_Q320.jpg

The perceptual machinery experiences some confusion at this image, despite the fact that the pure sense data never changes. You can 'perceive' two different images. If perception were built entirely from the ground up by the optical array, we shouldn't expect this confusion. Some other forces are contributing to how we perceive that image, which combined with the phenomenological account causes me to reject direct realism. I'm not a skeptic about the world, but I certainly don't think we have direct experience of things.

Regarding the experiment you discussed, I'd explain it via object permanence. It's been demonstrated in infants as young as 3-4 months, and is a function of the front cortex. Even higher mammals show this trait. It makes me think of A-not-B errors in child psychology. So you train a child to find a toy under box A for a few trials. Then in the last trial, with the child's attention, you put the toy under box B, which is also in reach. Children who are young enough will still reach for box A and fail the test. It demonstrates some working memory, but not object permanence. They remember the toy as being under A from being primed by that several times, but it does not register that the toy remains in box B, despite them seeing it placed there.

I think something similar occurs in the experiment you discussed. The mind maintains working memory of the original shape, so that across the texture change, the fully unchanged image still exists in the mind adjacently to the changing image. It is as if the mind is synthesizing both images in real time so that the illusion of two squares exists.

The example of this and of the illusion I provided show that perception is far more of a top-down process than Gibson wants to suggest, although I don't think it negates his theory about the sensory aspect of things.

All that said, I don't think that it matters. Gibson still points out that we are witnessing change. He specifies that we perceive invariants (objects) and events. What is an event if not something that occurs in time? There is a lot of language play happening here. I don't care whether we even apply the word time. We can call it something else. I'm willing to accept Gibson when he says we don't directly perceive time. That is trivially true. There is no time data or a time circuit in the body for measuring time. Time just is the duration between and elapsing across the change which encompasses an event. Change registers as time. Again, I hardly care what we think about time, only that it is irreducibly part of the structure of experience, and is necessary for any meaning.

In a timeless existence, it wouldn't make sense that any change that I undergo in a temporal existence could ever register to God. In fact, if there is any change at all in God, then an event elapses. Call it time, or don't. If this is not possible, then I'm unsure of how anything like a mental process could occur in this divine person, much less how the infinity of all events are supposed to register meaningfully in an instantaneous superposition.

For instance, Peace I know that you pray. Your prayer is an event. It elapses. It involves words, the meaning of which requires a syntax, i.e. some words have to come after other words. If the waveforms associated with each of those words were superimposed, the sentence would not have meaning. If God hears your prayer in a meaningful way, then we'd think He "hears" it at the moment you are uttering it (that is, it isn't translated into timeless God code). How do we make sense that God can hear and understand you when you pray if there is no time?
